_meta.schema: entry: id, world(ansible|rhel), category, intent, command, notes, mentor_note(optional), verify, undo, blast(green|yellow|red), tags[], source, verified

blast_legend.red: can touch the fleet or destroy data

entries.intent: Check a playbook for syntax errors without running it
entries.notes: Parses the playbook and its includes; catches YAML and playbook-keyword mistakes. Does NOT catch bad module arguments or missing files on targets.
entries.mentor_note: This is the authoritative YAML check — trust it over any offline linter, including this tool's.
entries.verify: Exit code 0 and the line 'playbook: site.yml' with no error output.

entries.intent: See what a playbook WOULD change without changing anything
entries.notes: Check mode predicts changed/ok per task; --diff shows file content changes. Modules with full check_mode support are accurate; command/shell tasks are skipped, so a --check run that looks clean can still change things for real.
entries.mentor_note: Trust it about 90%. The other 10% is command/shell tasks — read those by hand.
entries.verify: Output shows predicted changed= counts; nothing on the targets actually changed (spot-check one).
entries.undo: none — read-only (but see notes: not all modules honor check mode)

entries.intent: See exactly which hosts a play or pattern will hit
entries.notes: Expands the hosts: pattern of every play against your inventory and prints the matched hosts. Run this before anything red.
entries.verify: The printed host list matches what you intended — no extras.

entries.intent: See every task a playbook would run, in order
entries.notes: Prints plays and task names without executing. Pair with --list-tags to see what's skippable.
entries.verify: Task list prints; nothing executes.

entries.intent: See which config file is loaded and what differs from defaults
entries.notes: ansible --version prints the winning config file (precedence: $ANSIBLE_CONFIG, ./ansible.cfg, ~/.ansible.cfg, /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg). dump --only-changed shows every setting you've overridden and where it came from.
entries.mentor_note: A world-writable current directory makes Ansible silently skip ./ansible.cfg. If 'config file =' isn't what you expect, check directory permissions first.
entries.verify: 'config file =' points at the file you intend; each changed setting names its origin.

entries.intent: Run a playbook against only some of its hosts
entries.notes: --limit (or -l) intersects the play's hosts: pattern with your subset. Accepts names, groups, globs (web*), and comma lists. THE damage-containment flag: test on one host before the fleet.
entries.mentor_note: New change? --limit one host, verify, then widen. Every time. No exceptions, including Fridays.
entries.verify: Recap shows only the limited host(s).
entries.undo: n/a — limits scope; the tasks themselves still change state per their own undo

entries.intent: Target hosts with patterns: groups, exclusions, intersections
entries.notes: Patterns: 'a:b' union, 'a:!b' exclude, 'a:&b' intersection, 'web*' glob, 'all' everything. Quote the pattern — ! and & are shell characters.
entries.verify: Run with --list-hosts first to see the expansion.
entries.undo: none — pattern selection itself is read-only

entries.intent: Resume a long playbook at a specific task
entries.notes: Skips everything before the named task. Dangerous if earlier tasks set facts or prerequisites the later tasks assume — know what you're skipping.
entries.verify: First executed task in output is the one you named.
entries.undo: n/a — depends on the tasks run

entries.intent: Confirm each task interactively before it runs
entries.notes: Prompts y/n/c per task (c = continue without asking). Slow but surgical — good for a first run of someone else's playbook.
entries.verify: You get a (y/n/c) prompt before each task.

entries.intent: Run only tasks with a given tag
entries.notes: Drop --list-tasks to actually run. --skip-tags inverts. See available tags with --list-tags.
entries.verify: --list-tasks preview shows only the tagged tasks.
entries.undo: n/a — depends on the tasks run

entries.intent: Test that Ansible can reach and run Python on hosts
entries.notes: Not ICMP — it SSHes in and runs a tiny Python module. SUCCESS means transport AND Python module execution both work. If raw works but ping fails, the problem is Python-side (interpreter, temp dir), not SSH.
entries.mentor_note: This distinction — transport vs module execution — solved our first outage. Learn it cold.
entries.verify: Each host reports SUCCESS with "ping": "pong".

entries.intent: See exactly what Ansible is doing under the hood
entries.notes: -v result data, -vvv connection commands (the actual ssh/sftp invocations), -vvvv adds connection plugin debugging. Look for 'ESTABLISH SSH CONNECTION' vs 'ESTABLISH LOCAL CONNECTION' to see how a host is really being reached.
entries.mentor_note: A hang at a task usually means an invisible prompt — password, host key, or sudo. -vvv shows you the exact command it's stuck on; run that command yourself and you'll see the prompt.
entries.verify: Output includes ESTABLISH ... CONNECTION lines per task.
entries.undo: none — verbosity only; the run itself still changes state

entries.intent: See every variable Ansible has resolved for one host
entries.notes: Prints the merged variables (connection settings included) for that host as JSON. THE tool for 'why is it connecting like that?'. For localhost: if this returns anything without ansible_connection=local, delegation to localhost will SSH to your own box.
entries.verify: JSON shows the vars you expect; for localhost expect ansible_connection: local or no entry at all (implicit localhost).

entries.intent: See the whole inventory as a group tree
entries.notes: ASCII tree of groups and members. Add --vars to include variables (verbose). First command to run on an unfamiliar control node.
entries.verify: Tree prints; groups match expectations.

entries.intent: See facts (OS, IPs, memory) Ansible gathers about a host
entries.notes: setup is the fact-gathering module. filter= narrows the firehose. Common: ansible_default_ipv4, ansible_distribution*, ansible_memtotal_mb, ansible_mounts.
entries.verify: Facts print for the host.

entries.intent: Run one privileged command on hosts (ad-hoc)
entries.notes: -m command runs without a shell (no pipes/redirects; use -m shell if you need them). --become elevates, -K prompts for the sudo password. Without -K a sudo password requirement = silent hang.
entries.mentor_note: Forgetting -K is the #1 'Ansible is frozen' cause after host-key prompts.
entries.verify: Each host returns rc=0 and the command output.
entries.undo: depends on the command — prefer read-only commands ad-hoc

entries.intent: Control how many hosts run in parallel
entries.notes: Default forks is 5. Raise for speed on big fleets; LOWER it (even to 1, or use serial: in the play) for risky rolling changes so failures stop early.
entries.verify: With forks 1, hosts complete strictly one at a time in output.

entries.intent: Create or edit an encrypted secrets file
entries.notes: Opens $EDITOR, encrypts on save (AES256). Edit later with ansible-vault edit, view with ansible-vault view. At run time supply the password: --ask-vault-pass or --vault-password-file.
entries.mentor_note: Name encrypted files 'vault.yml' and reference their vars from a plain vars file — greppability without decryption.
entries.verify: File starts with $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256. ansible-vault view shows the plaintext.
entries.undo: ansible-vault decrypt <file> (permanently removes encryption — rarely what you want)

entries.intent: Encrypt a single value to paste into a vars file
entries.notes: Emits a !vault-tagged YAML block you paste inline; --stdin-name prompts for the secret so it never lands in shell history. (Passing the secret as an argument leaves it in ~/.bash_history — the real leak risk of this command.)
entries.mentor_note: If you already typed a secret on the command line: history -d that line, and rotate the secret if the box is shared.
entries.verify: Output is a db_password: !vault | block; a playbook using it decrypts correctly with the vault password. history | tail shows no plaintext secret.
entries.undo: replace the block with a plain value (and rotate the secret if it was exposed anywhere, including shell history)

entries.intent: Change the vault password on encrypted files
entries.notes: Prompts for old and new passwords. Do this on personnel change — the vault password is a shared secret.
entries.verify: ansible-vault view works with the new password and fails with the old.
entries.undo: rekey again back to a known password

entries.intent: Read the official docs for any module, offline, on the box
entries.notes: Full vendor documentation with examples, right on the control node. ansible-doc -l lists everything installed. -s prints a playbook-ready snippet skeleton.
entries.mentor_note: This is the authority this tool defers to. When my dictionaries and ansible-doc disagree, ansible-doc wins — it ships with your exact version.
entries.verify: Doc page renders in your pager.

entries.intent: See all disks, partitions, and mount points at a glance
entries.notes: Tree of block devices; -f adds filesystem type, label, UUID, and mountpoint. First command for any storage question.
entries.verify: Tree prints; devices match hardware expectations.

entries.intent: See how full each filesystem is
entries.notes: -h human sizes, -T shows filesystem type. A filesystem at 100% breaks services in weird ways (logs, PID files, sockets). Check /var and /tmp specifically.
entries.verify: Use% column readable; nothing unexpectedly at 100%.

entries.intent: Find what is eating the disk
entries.notes: -x stays on one filesystem (won't cross mounts), sort -rh ranks biggest first. Start at the mount df said was full.
entries.verify: Top offenders listed with sizes.

entries.intent: See LVM layout: physical volumes, volume groups, logical volumes
entries.notes: Three quick tables: disks in LVM (pvs), pools (vgs — check VFree for growth room), volumes (lvs). The LVM mental model: PV -> VG -> LV -> filesystem.
entries.verify: Tables print; VFree in vgs shows available headroom.

entries.intent: Grow a logical volume AND its filesystem in one step
entries.notes: -r (--resizefs) resizes the filesystem (xfs_growfs/resize2fs) in the same operation — the safe modern way. Requires free space in the VG (check vgs first). XFS can only grow, never shrink.
entries.mentor_note: Always -r. The classic outage is extending the LV, forgetting the filesystem, and wondering why df didn't change.
entries.verify: df -h shows the new size on the mount.
entries.undo: none for XFS (cannot shrink). Plan sizes carefully; ext4 shrink requires unmount and is expert territory.

entries.intent: Verify what is mounted where, with options
entries.notes: Tree of mounts; --verify checks /etc/fstab for errors WITHOUT rebooting — run it after every fstab edit, before the reboot finds your typo for you.
entries.verify: No [E] error lines in --verify output.

entries.intent: See why a service is dead or unhappy
entries.notes: State, PID, recent log lines. Loaded line shows the unit file path and enabled/disabled. Follow with journalctl -u sshd for full logs.
entries.verify: Active: line shows expected state.

entries.intent: Start a service now AND on every boot
entries.notes: enable wires the boot symlink; --now also starts it immediately. 'start' alone does NOT survive reboot — the classic gap.
entries.mentor_note: Quick check I give every student: systemctl start works but the service is dead after reboot — what did you forget? This flag.
entries.verify: systemctl is-enabled httpd -> enabled; systemctl is-active httpd -> active.

entries.intent: List everything that failed on this box
entries.notes: One-line health check. Follow each failure with systemctl status <unit> and journalctl -u <unit>. reset-failed clears the flag after you fix it.
entries.verify: '0 loaded units listed' when healthy.

entries.intent: Make systemd re-read unit files after editing one
entries.notes: Required after creating or editing any unit file. systemd warns about it but people miss the warning; symptoms are 'my edit did nothing'.
entries.verify: systemctl cat <unit> shows your edited content.

entries.intent: Override a vendor unit file without editing it in place
entries.notes: Creates a drop-in override in /etc/systemd/system/httpd.service.d/ — survives package updates, unlike editing /usr/lib/systemd/system directly. --full copies the whole unit instead.
entries.verify: systemctl cat httpd shows the drop-in appended.

entries.intent: See network devices and their connection state
entries.command: nmcli device status && nmcli connection show
entries.notes: NetworkManager is the RHEL network authority; nmcli is its CLI. Devices = hardware, connections = config profiles. A device 'disconnected' with a profile present usually means the profile isn't set to autoconnect.
entries.verify: Expected device shows 'connected' with the right profile.

entries.intent: See IP addresses, routes, and DNS quickly
entries.command: ip -br a && ip route && resolvectl status 2>/dev/null | head -20
entries.notes: -br is brief mode — one line per interface. ip route shows the default gateway; resolvectl shows DNS (on systemd-resolved systems; otherwise cat /etc/resolv.conf).
entries.verify: Addresses, default route, and DNS servers all present and sane.

entries.intent: See what is listening on which port, and who owns it
entries.notes: t TCP, u UDP, l listening, p process (needs root), n numeric. The modern netstat. 'Is the service actually listening?' answered in one line.
entries.verify: Expected daemon listed on expected port.

entries.intent: Check whether SELinux is enforcing
entries.notes: Enforcing/Permissive/Disabled. Permissive logs denials without blocking — the diagnostic mode. Never 'fix' a problem by disabling SELinux; find the denial and fix the label or boolean.
entries.mentor_note: If turning SELinux off 'fixes' it, you've found the cause, not the fix. Now go fix it properly.
entries.verify: Mode matches site policy (Enforcing in this shop).

entries.intent: Find recent SELinux denials and what they blocked
entries.notes: Reads the audit log for Access Vector Cache denials. Each record names the process (comm=), target, and contexts. Pipe a denial through audit2why for an explanation, audit2allow to draft a policy (review before applying!).
entries.verify: Denials print with timestamps, or 'no matches' when clean.

entries.intent: Fix wrong SELinux labels on files
entries.notes: Resets contexts to policy defaults. The #1 cause of 'service can't read its own files' after files were moved (mv preserves the old context; cp inherits the target's).
entries.verify: ls -Z shows expected contexts; the denial stops appearing in ausearch.
entries.undo: contexts return to policy defaults — if you needed a custom context, define it with semanage fcontext first

entries.intent: Permanently set the right SELinux context for a custom path
entries.notes: semanage records the rule in policy; restorecon applies it. chcon alone is temporary — a relabel wipes it. This pair is the permanent fix.
entries.verify: ls -Z /srv/site shows httpd_sys_content_t; survives touch /.autorelabel + reboot (or a restorecon).

entries.intent: Flip an SELinux boolean (e.g. let httpd make network connections)
entries.notes: -P persists across reboots. List candidates with getsebool -a | grep <service>. Booleans are the vendor-sanctioned tuning knobs — prefer them over custom policy.
entries.verify: getsebool httpd_can_network_connect -> on; the denial stops.

entries.intent: See the current firewall rules and active zones
entries.notes: --list-all shows the default zone's services, ports, and rich rules. Add --zone=<z> for others. Runtime and permanent configs are SEPARATE — what you see running may not survive reload.
entries.verify: State 'running'; rules match expectations.

entries.intent: Open a service or port, permanently and now
entries.notes: --permanent writes config but does NOT change the running firewall; --reload applies it. Without --permanent the rule vanishes at reload/reboot. The pair is the idiom. Ports: --add-port=8443/tcp.
entries.mentor_note: Every firewalld surprise in history is runtime-vs-permanent confusion. Say the pair out loud as one command.
entries.verify: firewall-cmd --list-services shows it; survives firewall-cmd --reload.

entries.intent: See a user's UID, groups, and SELinux context
entries.notes: Groups shown are current; a user added to a group mid-session must log out/in (or newgrp) to pick it up — the classic 'I added them to the group but it doesn't work'.
entries.verify: Expected groups listed.

entries.intent: Add a user to a group without destroying their other groups
entries.notes: -a APPENDS; -G alone REPLACES the supplementary group list — the most destructive missing letter in Linux administration. wheel = sudo rights on RHEL.
entries.mentor_note: usermod -G without -a has ended careers. The tool's generator will never emit it bare.
entries.verify: id alice shows wheel plus all previous groups.

entries.intent: Validate sudoers syntax before it locks everyone out
entries.notes: Checks /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/*. A syntax error in sudoers can disable sudo for the whole box. Always edit with visudo (it validates on save), never a bare editor.
entries.verify: 'parsed OK' for every file.

entries.intent: See who logged in recently, and failed attempts
entries.notes: last reads /var/log/wtmp (successes), lastb reads btmp (failures, needs root). Failed-login spikes are your first breach indicator.
entries.verify: Entries print; investigate anything unfamiliar.

entries.intent: Read the logs for one service
entries.notes: journald is the structured log store; -u filters by unit. --since/--until take natural-ish dates ('yesterday', '2026-08-23 14:00'). Add -f to follow live.
entries.verify: Log lines for the unit print in the window requested.

entries.intent: See every error since the last boot
entries.notes: -p err filters priority error and worse; -b limits to this boot (-b -1 = previous boot — gold after an unexplained reboot). -xe adds explanations and jumps to the end.
entries.verify: Errors print or the list is empty (healthy).

entries.intent: Install a package
entries.notes: Resolves dependencies from configured repos (dnf repolist to see them; air-gapped boxes point at a local mirror). -y skips the confirm — leave it OFF for anything you haven't read.
entries.verify: rpm -q httpd shows the installed version.

entries.intent: See what package operations happened, and roll one back
entries.notes: Every transaction is numbered. undo reverses installs/removals of that transaction (config edits stay). 'What changed on this box last Tuesday?' — dnf history info <id>.
entries.verify: dnf history info <id> shows the undo transaction; affected packages back at prior versions.
entries.undo: dnf history undo of the undo itself

entries.intent: Find which package owns a file
entries.notes: Reverse lookup: file -> package. Pair with rpm -V <pkg> to check whether packaged files were modified (config drift/tamper check), and dnf provides '*/somefile' to find not-yet-installed owners.
entries.verify: Package name prints.

entries.intent: Find what is eating CPU or memory
entries.notes: Sort by -%mem or -%cpu. For live view: top (shift-M sorts by memory). free -h for the memory headline — remember 'available', not 'free', is the number that matters (buff/cache gives memory back on demand).
entries.verify: Top consumers listed; investigate surprises.

entries.intent: Stop a runaway process, gently then firmly
entries.command: kill <pid>       # then, only if ignored:  kill -9 <pid>
entries.notes: Plain kill sends SIGTERM — a polite 'clean up and exit'. -9 (SIGKILL) is uncatchable: no cleanup, possible corrupted state. If it's a service, systemctl stop is the right door, not kill.
entries.mentor_note: kill -9 first is like unplugging the server to close a program. It's on the Forbidden List as a habit; as a last resort it's a tool.
entries.verify: ps -p <pid> returns nothing.
entries.undo: restart the process/service; check for leftover lock/PID files if it was -9'd

entries.intent: Find files by name, age, or size
entries.notes: -mtime +30 = modified >30 days ago; -size +100M = bigger than 100MB. ALWAYS run bare (printing matches) before adding -delete or -exec — see the Forbidden List.
entries.verify: The printed list is exactly what you expect before acting on it.
entries.undo: none for the search; -delete is unrecoverable — that's why we look first

entries.intent: Archive a directory (backup before you touch it)
entries.notes: c create, z gzip, f file. Verify with tar -tzf <file> (list) before trusting it. Extract with tar -xzf, add -C /target to choose destination.
entries.mentor_note: The pre-change /etc tarball has saved me more times than every monitoring system combined. Cheap insurance, take it.
entries.verify: tar -tzf lists the expected contents; file size is non-trivial.
entries.undo: rm the archive (it's a copy; the originals were never touched)

entries.intent: See a file's exact permissions, owner, and timestamps
entries.notes: stat gives octal mode, owner, and all three timestamps; ls -Z adds SELinux context. The full identity card of a file — check before AND after permission changes.
entries.verify: Mode/owner/context match the vendor or STIG expectation.

entries.intent: Install a collection offline (air-gapped, from a carried tarball)
entries.notes: Collections (ansible.posix, community.general...) are NOT part of ansible-core — they install separately, and on an air-gapped box the tarball must be carried across. Download low-side with 'ansible-galaxy collection download <name>', transfer, install from the file path. Installs to ~/.ansible/collections by default.
entries.mentor_note: Two snippets in this kit (authorized_key, firewalld module) need ansible.posix — check for it on day one, not mid-change.
entries.verify: ansible-galaxy collection list shows the collection and version; ansible-doc ansible.posix.firewalld renders.

entries.intent: Pull a file OFF remote hosts for evidence (compare configs across the fleet)
entries.notes: fetch is copy in reverse: grabs src from every matched host into dest/<hostname>/<path> locally. THE evidence-gathering move — pull the suspect config from 50 hosts and diff them before pushing any fix. For a quick in-memory peek at one file, -m slurp returns it base64-encoded instead.
entries.mentor_note: Diagnose with fetch before you treat with copy. Reading the fleet's actual state has saved me from 'fixing' the wrong thing more times than I can count.
entries.verify: evidence/<host>/etc/ssh/sshd_config exists per host; diff -r evidence/web01 evidence/web02 shows the drift you're hunting.
entries.undo: rm -r evidence/ locally — targets were never written to

entries.intent: Stand up or repair a local dnf repository (air-gapped)
entries.command:
createrepo_c /srv/repo/rhel9-baseos
printf '[local-baseos]
name=Local BaseOS
baseurl=file:///srv/repo/rhel9-baseos
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
' > /etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo
dnf clean all && dnf repolist
entries.notes: createrepo_c builds/refreshes the repodata metadata over a directory of RPMs; the .repo file points dnf at it (file:// for local, http:// for a mirror host). Re-run createrepo_c after adding RPMs. gpgcheck=1 with the imported RH GPG key keeps package integrity honest even offline.
entries.mentor_note: When 'Failed to download metadata' strikes on an air-gapped box, it's almost always this layer: stale repodata or a wrong baseurl path. This block is the repair kit.
entries.verify: dnf repolist shows the repo with a package count; dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=local-baseos install <pkg> resolves.

entries.intent: Check time sync health (chrony)
entries.notes: tracking shows the current offset and which source the clock is disciplined to; sources lists candidates (the * marks the selected one). On air-gapped enclaves the source is a local NTP server or GPS clock — drift breaks Kerberos, TLS, 2FA, and makes cross-host log timelines lie.
entries.verify: Leap status 'Normal'; System time offset well under a second; one source marked with *.

entries.intent: Cap the journal's disk usage permanently (after a cleanup)
entries.command:
journalctl --disk-usage
mkdir -p /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d
printf '[Journal]\nSystemMaxUse=500M\n' > /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/size.conf
systemctl restart systemd-journald
entries.notes: The disk-full tree says it: don't just delete — cap. --vacuum-size=500M does the one-time cleanup; the drop-in makes the cap permanent so the appointment never recurs. Drop-in beats editing journald.conf directly (survives updates).
entries.verify: journalctl --disk-usage stays at or under the cap over the following days.

entries.intent: Check or debug log rotation for classic /var/log files
entries.notes: -d is dry-run debug: shows every log file logrotate manages and what it WOULD do, changing nothing. Per-service policies live in /etc/logrotate.d/. A service spamming /var/log with no rotation policy is the other half of every disk-full story.
entries.verify: The runaway log file appears in the -d output with a sane rotate/size policy; after the daily timer runs, dated/compressed siblings exist.

entries.intent: Restore from a tar backup — safely, to a staging area first
entries.command:
tar -tzf etc-backup-2026-08-24.tar.gz | head
mkdir -p /tmp/restore-test
tar -xzf etc-backup-2026-08-24.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore-test
diff -r /tmp/restore-test/etc/ssh /etc/ssh | head
entries.notes: List first (-t), extract into a STAGING directory (-C), diff against live, then copy over only what you mean to restore. Never extract an absolute-path archive as root onto / — one wrong archive overwrites the living system. --strip-components=N trims leading path levels when needed.
entries.mentor_note: A backup that has never been restore-tested is a rumor. This staging pattern IS the restore test — run it before you need it.
entries.verify: Staged tree matches expectations; the specific files you copy back diff clean afterward.
entries.undo: rm -r /tmp/restore-test (staging is disposable; live files only change when you copy them, deliberately)

entries.intent: Mount an NFS share, now and at boot
entries.command:
showmount -e 192.168.1.117
mkdir -p /mnt/vault
mount -t nfs 192.168.1.117:/srv/shares/vault /mnt/vault
echo '192.168.1.117:/srv/shares/vault /mnt/vault nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0' >> /etc/fstab
findmnt --verify
entries.notes: showmount -e lists what the server exports (needs nfs-utils). _netdev in fstab makes boot wait for the network before mounting — without it, boots race the network and land in emergency mode. SELinux gotcha: services reading NFS content often need a boolean (getsebool -a | grep nfs).
entries.verify: findmnt /mnt/vault shows the mount; findmnt --verify passes; after reboot the mount returns.
entries.undo: umount /mnt/vault && remove the fstab line && findmnt --verify
